name: Possessiveness (parigraha)
description: Holding possessions, living or lifeless — the bond the Sūtrakṛtāṅga names first; defined in both traditions as attachment (mūrcchā), though the Digambaras hold any clothing to show it and the Śvetāmbaras do not.

name: Attachment (mūrcchā)
description: Infatuation with what one has — the inner essence of possessiveness ('possession is attachment'); one who gives up the thought 'mine' gives up what is his.

name: Attachment and aversion (pejja-dosa, rāga-dveṣa)
description: The two roots of karma under which the four passions are gathered (deceit and greed as attachment, anger and pride as aversion); 'attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma'.

name: Attachment even to the good (praśasta-rāga)
description: Even affection for the teacher binds: Gautama's love for Mahāvīra delayed his omniscience until the night of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa, when he cut that bond.
antidotes: reflection on the Jina's own detachment

name: The thirty-three disrespects to the teacher (āśātanā)
description: Faults of a pupil toward teacher and elders — walking ahead of or too close to them, sitting higher, speaking before them, eating first, not answering when called, and so on — listed in the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The twenty-one grave faults (śabala)
description: Faults that 'spot' a monk's conduct, such as accepting food prepared for him, eating at night, repeated minor violations of vows — listed in the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The twenty grounds of disturbed concentration (asamādhi-sthāna)
description: Careless conduct that disturbs concentration — walking hastily, not inspecting the ground, using too large a seat, quarrelling, speaking at wrong times, and so on — listed in the first chapter of the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The thirty grounds of deluding karma
description: Acts so grave that they bind the strongest deluding karma — killing beings cruelly, betraying a teacher or the community, falsely claiming to be a monk or omniscient, and others — listed in the ninth chapter of the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The eighteen sources of sin (pāpa-sthānaka)
description: Recited in Śvetāmbara confession: violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, possessiveness, anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, aversion, quarrelling, false accusation, slander, pleasure and displeasure, disparaging others, deceitful falsehood, and the thorn of wrong faith.
